clinical: Atherosclerosis starts in the intima, where LDL cholesterol collects beneath a damaged endothelium and forms fatty streaks that can grow into plaques.
Smoking, high blood pressure and high LDL cholesterol all injure the endothelium and reduce its nitric oxide release, an early step in atherosclerosis.

Tunica media.description: The tunica media is the thick middle coat of an elastic artery. It is made of repeated lamellar units: a sheet of elastin with smooth muscle cells, collagen and ground substance between each pair of sheets. The smooth muscle cells make the elastin and collagen, and the elastic sheets stretch in systole and recoil in diastole to keep blood flowing.
clinical: Marfan syndrome, caused by a fibrillin-1 defect, weakens the elastic lamellae of the media, causing cystic medial degeneration, aortic dilation and a risk of dissection.
With age and long-standing hypertension the elastic lamellae fragment and the aorta stiffens, which raises systolic pressure and pulse pressure.

Tunica adventitia.description: The tunica adventitia is the outer coat of the aorta, made of connective tissue: wavy type I collagen bundles with elastic fibres, fibroblasts, nerves and small vessels. Its collagen limits how far the wall can stretch. The aortic wall is too thick to be fed from the lumen alone, so small vessels called vasa vasorum run through the outer wall to supply it.
clinical: When an aneurysm or dissection tears through the adventitia, blood escapes into the pericardium, mediastinum or pleural cavity, which is life-threatening.
Tertiary syphilis inflames the vasa vasorum of the ascending aorta; the resulting loss of medial elastic tissue weakens the wall and can produce an aneurysm.
Red cells lose their biconcave shape and become spherical, so the spleen removes them early, causing haemolytic anaemia.
Defective beta-2 integrins stop leukocytes from sticking to the endothelium and leaving the blood, so affected patients get recurrent bacterial infections.

parts.description: The endothelium is the single layer of flat (simple squamous) cells that lines the inside (lumen) of every blood vessel, resting on a basement membrane. Its cells release nitric oxide and prostacyclin, which relax the vessel and discourage platelets from sticking, and endothelin, which constricts it. They also store von Willebrand factor in Weibel–Palade bodies and regulate which leukocytes can leave the blood. In a section, look for thin, flattened nuclei that bulge slightly into the lumen.

The subendothelial layer is the loose connective-tissue zone of the intima (the innermost coat of the wall), lying between the endothelium and the first elastic lamellae. In the aorta it is relatively thick in adults and contains collagen, elastic fibres, proteoglycans (water-binding ground substance) and scattered smooth muscle cells, sometimes called myointimal cells. It thickens with age, and it is where lipid-laden fatty streaks and atherosclerotic plaques begin to form.

The internal elastic lamina is the sheet of elastin that forms the boundary between the tunica intima and the tunica media. In muscular arteries it is a prominent, wavy, fenestrated (perforated) band that stands out on an elastic stain, but in a large elastic artery such as the aorta it is inconspicuous and looks like just the first of the medial elastic lamellae. Its fenestrae allow small molecules to diffuse from the lumen into the media.

Elastic lamellae are the concentric, wavy sheets of elastin that form most of the tunica media in an elastic artery such as the aorta. Each sheet is fenestrated (perforated), and smooth muscle cells, collagen and ground substance fill the spaces between successive sheets. On an elastic stain such as Verhoeff–van Gieson they appear as dark, concentric wavy lines, and their elasticity lets the wall stretch in systole and recoil in diastole.

The external elastic lamina is the elastic layer at the outer edge of the tunica media, separating the media from the tunica adventitia. In muscular arteries it is a distinct, wavy band that stands out on an elastic stain, whereas in a large elastic artery such as the aorta it is poorly defined and blends with the outermost lamellae. This makes the exact outer limit of the media hard to pinpoint in such vessels.

The external elastic lamina is the outermost elastic sheet of the tunica media, lying just inside the adventitia and separating the smooth muscle layers from the collagen-rich outer coat. It is usually thinner and less regular than the internal elastic lamina, so it is easy to miss in a section. Look for a wavy dark band at the outer edge of the media, with the loose, pink collagen of the adventitia lying beyond it.

Adventitial collagen bundles are the thick, wavy bundles of type I collagen that form most of the tunica adventitia, the outer coat of the artery. They run lengthwise and obliquely among elastic fibres, and their crimped shape lets the wall stretch only a little before the collagen resists further stretch. In haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) sections they look pink and wavy; on Verhoeff–van Gieson stain they are red, unlike the black elastic fibres.

Vasa vasorum (Latin for 'vessels of the vessels') are the small arteries, veins and capillaries that run through the outer wall of large vessels such as the aorta. They supply the outer media and adventitia, which are too thick to be fed by diffusion from the lumen alone, while the inner media is nourished from the blood inside the vessel. In a section, look for small, thin-walled vessels containing red cells in the adventitia.

Vasa vasorum venules are the small veins of the vasa vasorum network, lying in the adventitia and outer media of large arteries. They collect blood after it has passed through the capillaries of the outer wall and drain it into larger veins of the adventitia. Their wall is thinner than that of the neighbouring arterioles and contains little smooth muscle, so in a section they look like wide, thin-walled channels, often with red cells inside.

Nervi vasorum (Latin for 'nerves of the vessels') are small autonomic nerve fibres that run in the adventitia and outer media of large arteries. They are mainly sympathetic, releasing noradrenaline to control the smooth muscle of the wall and to regulate the vasa vasorum. In a section they appear as small, pale bundles of axons lying among the collagen of the adventitia, close to the vasa vasorum.

Perivascular fat is the layer of adipose (fatty) tissue that surrounds the outside of the artery, lying just beyond the tunica adventitia. It cushions the vessel, stores energy, and releases signalling molecules such as adiponectin that can influence the smooth muscle of the wall. In a section, look for clusters of large, pale fat cells that appear almost empty, each with a thin rim of cytoplasm and a flattened nucleus pushed to one side.

Red blood cells (erythrocytes) are biconcave, anucleate (nucleus-free) discs about 7.5 µm across. Their thin, dish-shaped form gives a large surface area for gas exchange, and haemoglobin inside them carries most of the oxygen. Their flexibility lets them fold through capillaries narrower than their own diameter. In haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) sections they look like pink, round cells with a pale centre and no nucleus.

A rolling leukocyte is a white blood cell, most often a neutrophil, that slows and rolls along the inner lining of a vessel during inflammation. Selectins on the endothelium first tether it and make it roll, then integrins make it stop and squeeze between endothelial cells into the tissue, a process called diapedesis. This happens mainly in postcapillary venules, the small veins just downstream of the capillaries. In a section, neutrophils are identified by their multilobed nucleus and pale, granular cytoplasm.
